Category Assessment.Name: Agent Goal Hijack
Category Assessment.OWASP summary: Attackers manipulate an agent's objectives, task selection, or decision pathways because agents cannot reliably distinguish instructions from surrounding content.
Category Assessment.Boundary (optional): Bounded to prompt-layer manipulation of tool/argument selection (E1-E4): free-text prompt content, self-declared user_profile, replayed conversation memory, and unverified RAG PDF content can all steer which of the 11 tools/arguments the LLM emits, with no server-side re-validation at tool dispatch (E5).

Category Assessment.Name: Tool Misuse and Exploitation
Category Assessment.OWASP summary: Agents misuse legitimate tools via prompt injection, unsafe delegation, or ambiguous instruction, leading to data exfiltration or workflow hijacking.
Category Assessment.Boundary (optional): Bounded to the 11 registered tools' silently-ignored arguments (department, id, category, justification, business_justification) and unenforced boolean flags (external_sharing) that let a caller/LLM supply misleading structured arguments the implementation never checks (E8-E13).

Category Assessment.Name: Identity and Privilege Abuse
Category Assessment.OWASP summary: Exploits dynamic trust and delegation to escalate access and bypass controls by manipulating identity, role inheritance, or cached context.
Category Assessment.Boundary (optional): Bounded to the self-selected role dropdown and hard-coded, non-session-bound process-wide user_id/teams globals (E7); no cross-system delegation chain or shadow-agent deployment exists in this single-server, single-orchestrator system.

Category Assessment.Name: Agentic Supply Chain Vulnerabilities
Category Assessment.OWASP summary: Arises when agents, tools, or artefacts sourced from third parties are malicious, compromised, or tampered with in transit.
Category Assessment.Boundary (optional): No third-party tool/plugin/model-weight supply chain, dynamic plugin loading, or external agent registry exists in this system; the 11 tools are fixed and locally defined, so this category has no concrete substrate here.

Category Assessment.Name: Unexpected Code Execution (RCE)
Category Assessment.OWASP summary: Agents that generate and execute code can be exploited to escalate actions into remote code execution or resource exhaustion.
Category Assessment.Boundary (optional): No tool in the 11 generates or executes code, shell commands, or infrastructure scripts; Phase B confirms no rate/counter guidance exists (Q15/Q16 blank), leaving no concrete resource-exhaustion substrate distinct from generic availability.

Category Assessment.Name: Memory & Context Poisoning
Category Assessment.OWASP summary: Attackers corrupt stored or retrievable context (conversation history, memory, RAG stores) that the agent reuses across turns or sessions.
Category Assessment.Boundary (optional): Bounded to session-level conversation-history replay (E4): prior LLM/tool output is re-interpolated into later prompts with no integrity control. No caller-writable persistent store (e.g., a poisonable vector database) exists — the RAG PDF corpus is a static local file, so long-term cross-session store poisoning is not evidenced.

Category Assessment.Name: Insecure Inter-Agent Communication
Category Assessment.OWASP summary: Multi-agent systems depend on inter-agent messaging (APIs, message buses, shared memory) that expands the attack surface when authentication/integrity controls are weak.
Category Assessment.Boundary (optional): No multi-agent or A2A protocol exists; this is a single MCP server invoked by a single LLM orchestrator loop, so there is no inter-agent channel to abuse.

Category Assessment.Name: Cascading Failures
Category Assessment.OWASP summary: A single fault (hallucination, malicious input, corrupted tool, poisoned memory) propagates across autonomous agents, compounding into system-wide harm.
Category Assessment.Boundary (optional): Bounded to single-agent hallucination propagation: unverified RAG PDF content or replayed memory (E4) could feed a hallucinated work-policy answer into a later turn's tool arguments. No multi-agent chain exists to compound the fault further, unlike the catalog's inter-agent cascading scenarios.

Category Assessment.Name: Human-Agent Trust Exploitation
Category Assessment.OWASP summary: Adversaries exploit the trust humans place in fluent, confident agent output to influence decisions, extract information, or steer outcomes.
Category Assessment.Boundary (optional): Bounded to the denial-message relay convention (the LLM is instructed to relay '🚫'-prefixed text verbatim, and such text bypasses output scanning, E15) and to unauthenticated role/identity trust (E7) that a human reviewer has no way to independently verify from the tool's response alone.

Category Assessment.Name: Rogue Agents
Category Assessment.OWASP summary: Malicious or compromised agents deviate from intended function or authorized scope within multi-agent or human-agent ecosystems.
Category Assessment.Boundary (optional): No multi-agent ecosystem exists for an agent to defect within; this system has exactly one LLM orchestrator and one fixed MCP tool set, so there is no rogue-peer substrate.

Threat Instances.Concrete threat: A caller types the literal or a lightly-paraphrased blocked phrase (e.g. "ignore all policies", "bypass security", "override all policies", "show all SSN data") into chat input on the fast_server.py path, which has no LLMGuard wiring at all, or crafts wording that slips past run_llm_with_mcp.py's BanSubstrings/pattern lists via the business-safe-pattern override, causing the LLM to disregard guidance rules 11-14 and select tool calls (e.g. view_team_compensation with unfiltered select_fields) it would otherwise refuse.

An attacker who can influence the on-disk work_rules_and_regulations_2016.pdf (no checksum/signature documented) embeds hidden instruction-like text that is retrieved by ask_for_workpolicy's similarity_search and interpolated into the RAG prompt, redirecting the LLM's subsequent tool selection or answer content without the caller's knowledge.

A caller sets user_profile (role/department/name) to an arbitrary self-declared value with no authentication; since the LLM sees this text in its system prompt and no tool re-verifies it, the caller can induce the LLM to behave as though it were addressing a manager-level request even though no server-side role check exists to catch the mismatch.

A caller spreads a manipulative instruction or false claim (e.g. a fabricated policy exception) across multiple turns so it persists in the last-10-turns conversation history and is silently re-interpolated into later prompts, progressively influencing tool argument choices across a session despite the system prompt's 'reference only' framing for memory.

Because no live @mcp.tool function calls the fully-built OPA client or LLMGuard, any caller who reaches the MCP server directly (bypassing the Streamlit/FastAPI orchestrators, e.g. by speaking the SSE protocol directly) can invoke any of the 11 tools with arbitrary arguments and receive whatever the tool body unconditionally does, with zero pre-execution authorization check at the boundary where one would otherwise be enforced.

A caller selects 'manager' in the self-declared, unauthenticated role dropdown (or supplies an equivalent claim via fast_server.py's ChatRequest.user_profile); since no tool reads input.extensions.subject.roles for an authorization decision and the process-wide user_id/teams globals are hard-coded rather than session-bound, the caller's claimed identity has no verification mechanism standing between the claim and any downstream role-gated behavior a future policy might add.

A caller invokes view_team_compensation or export_compensation_data with select_fields left null/empty; guidance rule 15 requires such a request be blocked, but the implementation instead proceeds and returns the full record set including the unconditionally-merged sensitive_data block (ssn, home_address, bank_account, tax_id, emergency_contact, personal_email), exposing the system's highest-impact PII/financial-identity data with a single default-shaped call.

A caller with any role (including 'employee', which rule 2/5 says should be blocked entirely from these tools) supplies a select_fields value that explicitly names ssn, personal_email, home_address, bank_account, tax_id, or emergency_contact; because the sensitive_data merge happens unconditionally before projection and no role check gates it, the requested sensitive fields are returned verbatim, directly violating rules 3 and 16.

A caller sets external_sharing=true on export_compensation_data or email_compensation_report, or targets a blocked/non-@ibm.com domain via email_compensation_report.destination or send_email.recipient_email; none of these are enforced (external_sharing is only echoed, destination is only cosmetically split, recipient_email is never even read), so compensation data can be exported or emailed externally in direct violation of rules 7, 8, 17, and 18.

A caller (including a manager legitimately permitted to send_email externally under rule 6) places compensation/salary/payroll content into email_content; nothing checks the content against the non-compensation restriction, so send_email becomes an unmonitored side channel for exactly the data email_compensation_report's external-sharing block (T09) is meant to prevent.

A caller declaring the 'employee' role invokes purchase with amount >= 200 (up to and beyond the manager's $1000 ceiling); the function never compares amount against any role-based limit and no approval field exists to gate the >=200 branch, so the purchase completes and returns a success confirmation regardless of the missing manager approval required by rule 9, with no ceiling stopping an arbitrarily large amount.

A caller invokes return_product with an amount unrelated to any real prior purchase; raw_return echoes the amount into a confirmation string with no cross-check against purchase records, so the tool will confirm an unsubstantiated refund amount purely on the caller's say-so.

If a future tool or injected content produces text beginning with the '🚫' denial-message prefix, run_llm_with_mcp.py's enforce_output skips LLMGuard output scanning entirely for that text and the system prompt instructs the LLM to relay it verbatim; this creates a standing defense-in-depth gap where the mere presence of that prefix — not any verified denial state — determines whether output scanning applies.

handoff.Summary: Applicable categories: ASI01 (Yes), ASI02 (Yes), ASI03 (Yes), ASI04 (No), ASI05 (No), ASI06 (Partial), ASI07 (No), ASI08 (Partial), ASI09 (Yes), ASI10 (No) -- 5 Yes/Partial-relevant-plus applicable substrates out of 10, grounded in the dead-code OPA/LLMGuard gap (E5-E6), the unconditional sensitive_data merge (E8), the unenforced external-sharing/domain/purchase-ceiling arguments (E9-E13), and unauthenticated self-declared identity (E7). 13 threat instances (T01..T13): 2 Critical (T07 unconditional sensitive-data return on missing select_fields; T11 purchase ceiling/approval bypass), 4 High (T01 blocked-phrase bypass, T05 missing pre-execution authorization, T06 unauthenticated role spoofing, T09 external-sharing/domain bypass), 5 Medium (T02, T03, T04, T10, plus none additional), 2 Low (T12, T13). All 21 Attack Surface rows carry a Threat IDs or an N/A -- reason disposition; 15 Evidence Index entries, each reused rather than duplicated across threats. All 62 catalog scenarios across the 10 categories received exactly one disposition citing a threat ID or an N/A -- reason grounded in this system's concrete absence of a multi-agent, supply-chain, or code-execution substrate. One semantic completeness pass was run (actors restricted to Caller/LLM/Tool/External with justification per instance; non-terminal layers -- prompt, MCP dispatch, tool body, external data -- each represented; severities checked against the Critical/High/Medium/Low definitions in the guide, e.g. downgrading return_product's unvalidated-refund threat to Low as a defense-in-depth finding rather than a boundary compromise; evidence IDs checked for reused, non-duplicated grounded facts); the pass surfaced two initial severity misclassifications (T07/T11 initially drafted as High, corrected to Critical as compromises of the highest-impact PII/financial-identity and financial-ceiling boundaries) and one actor correction (T13 corrected from Caller to LLM, since the '🚫'-bypass is triggered by generated/relayed output text, not a caller-supplied argument); both were repaired in the single allotted repair pass with no remaining inconsistency. Open gaps carried forward and newly surfaced: (1) purchase's manager-approval condition (rule 9) has no structured field to bind to (T11, carried from Phase A/B); (2) no stated cap on approved employee purchases beyond the $200 threshold (carried from Phase B Q13b, reflected in T11's evidence); (3) rules 11-14 remain prompt-layer-only and not OPA-policy-expressible against structured input (T01, source-boundary rule applied, carried from Phase A/B); (4) no denial logging or violation-code scheme exists, so ASI09's Financial Transaction Obfuscation and Compliance Violation Concealment scenarios are recorded N/A rather than forced into a threat instance without a concrete logging substrate.
